messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Martin Weiss is a 66-year-old software engineer who came to treatment after decades of telling himself that what happened in childhood was over and best left unexamined. He grew up with a caregiver who could turn violent without warning. What has stayed with him most vividly is not a single story he recites straight through, but fragments organized around the body: the shock of being grabbed, the feel of temperature on his skin just before or during an assault, and the sudden pounding in his chest when he sensed danger coming. As a boy he learned to scan small details that might tell him what was about to happen, because there was no reliable safety in the home and no one he felt he could trust.

In the years since, those fragments have remained strangely alive. A particular temperature on his skin can stop him cold before he has even put words to why. Sometimes it is simply the feel of cool air from the office vent across his forearms, or the abrupt contrast of hot water in the shower, and a memory of the abuse comes into his mind with no warning. Just as often, he notices his own heart racing and that sensation itself becomes the cue: the pounding is enough to pull up the old scene. When that happens, his body reacts before his mind has caught up. He becomes instantly alert, his muscles tighten, and his eyes move through the room for anything that could be used as a weapon, as if the past danger were present again.

Those moments do more than frighten him; they confirm what he has come to believe about the world and his place in it. When a memory breaks in because of a bodily sensation, Martin is certain it proves that you can never relax, that you have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next. He reads these reactions as evidence that other people are fundamentally unsafe and that he has remained outside ordinary human trust. Even in his marriage, he says there is a part of him that stands apart, watching. The old memories arrive with the force of something still unresolved, and he takes their return as proof that he is permanently an outsider now.

Those beliefs have shaped the way he lives. Because he mistrusts people and assumes danger can come at any moment, Martin avoids physical contact whenever he can. If a coworker reaches to pat his shoulder in congratulations, he flinches sharply; over time he has learned to keep more distance so no one gets close enough to touch him unexpectedly. At work, where he spends most days as a software engineer, he chooses a seat where no one can approach from behind and keeps his interactions clipped and functional. He has also withdrawn from social contact with people he used to see more easily, preferring not to put himself in situations where others might close the distance, ask personal questions, or reach toward him casually. He does not like attending to his own body either; he avoids looking at it closely or focusing on internal sensations, as though noticing too much might open a door he is trying to keep shut.

But the life he has built around avoidance has hardened the same convictions that drive it. The less he allows touch, the stranger and more intrusive it feels, which confirms his sense that he does not belong with other people. The more he pulls back from social contact, the more he experiences himself as separate and unable to trust. Avoiding his body has not made him feel less vulnerable; if anything, ordinary signs like his heart racing feel more abrupt and menacing when they break through his attention. Then he is even more convinced that he must stay vigilant.

That vigilance is nearly constant now. He notices dangerous objects in any environment before he notices comfort: a heavy stapler in a conference room, kitchen knives at home left too close to the edge, metal tools in the garage. His body often jolts at unexpected touch before he has had time to think who is there. Once he is in that state, the triggers multiply. The pounding heart he fears becomes louder in his awareness, and that sensation calls up more intrusive fragments. A change in temperature on his skin can do the same. The more watchful he becomes, the more easily these cues find him; the more he avoids, the less chance he has to discover that not every sensation means danger.

His wife finally urged him to seek help after he recoiled when she touched him from behind in their kitchen and then spent the evening withdrawn and ashamed. Martin came in because he is tired of living as if threat is always one step ahead of him. What frightens him most is the idea that this is simply who he is now—cut off, suspicious, always braced. What he hopes, though he says it cautiously, is that he might learn how to be in his own body and with other people without feeling that danger is already there.

violation_explanations: The vignette does not clearly state that triggers or reminders themselves lead Martin to negative appraisals; it says memories breaking in because of bodily sensations confirm beliefs, but not that triggers directly drive those appraisals.

The vignette does not clearly describe Martin’s negative appraisals causing triggers to arise or become more salient; triggers are described as bodily sensations and environmental cues, but not as being generated by his beliefs.
